expected_evidence: Geological: stratigraphic sediment cores/lake varves at the ~12,900 cal BP (Younger Dryas Boundary) horizon showing microspherule layers, with geochemical (SEM-EDS, isotopic) data indicating terrestrial/anthropogenic/biogenic origin (e.g., fungal spherules, framboidal pyrite, industrial fly-ash contamination) rather than cosmic origin

Material: independently collected and re-analyzed microspherule samples from multiple labs (e.g., failed replication attempts such as Surovell et al. 2009, Pinter et al. 2011, Holliday & Meltzer 2010, van Hoesel et al. 2013) showing inconsistent spatial/stratigraphic distribution or compositional mismatch with extraterrestrial material

Astronomical: absence of corroborating cosmic-impact signatures expected from an airburst - no confirmed impact crater, no shocked quartz, no statistically significant iridium/platinum-group-element anomaly matching bolide composition, no nanodiamond confirmation across independent labs

Model_prior (scientific literature): published peer-reviewed critiques and meta-analyses of the Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis documenting methodological problems, non-reproducibility, and alternative (non-cosmic) explanations for the microspherule concentrations
response.rationale: The interval (-10950) corresponds to the Younger Dryas onset, so I mapped detectability using the 'younger-dryas' row (material 0.35, geological 0.65, astronomical 0.7, model_prior 0.3). However, this hypothesis is not about a hard-to-recover prehistoric artifact but about a modern scientific controversy: whether physical/geochemical evidence for the Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis (microspherules, purportedly cosmic) has been refuted. This kind of evidence is preserved in well-studied sedimentary/lake-core archives across North America and has already been repeatedly sampled and analyzed with modern instrumentation (SEM-EDS, isotope geochemistry), and the refutation debate is documented in peer-reviewed literature (Pinter et al. 2011, Holliday & Meltzer 2010, Surovell et al. 2009, van Hoesel et al. 2013, among others - flagged here as model-prior recollection rather than verified from provided evidence text). Because the underlying record is geological/sedimentary rather than perishable organic/cultural material, and because it has been the subject of sustained modern scientific scrutiny with many independent replication attempts, actual detectability is higher than the raw table average across categories would suggest. I therefore adjust the composite detectability upward to ~0.6, reflecting strong geological and model_prior/literature channels but with material and low textual/oral_tradition/linguistic channels still constrained by the antiquity of the depositional record and total absence of writing at this period. A failure to find fully decisive evidence in the primary provided evidence text should not be read as strong evidence against the refutation - it may reflect that this is a live, evolving scientific debate rather than a settled archaeological fact, and the low-tier model-prior recollections about the debate should not be treated as established without independent verification.
